newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian jobs seen falling in Sept.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian jobs seen falling in Sept.

text.p: Australian markets will receive an update on data seen as crucial to the prospects for another cut in official interest rates when September labour force data is released on Thursday.
And for the interest rate bulls, the news is likely to be favourable.
Employment is expected to record its first fall in six months, and the unemployment rate is expected to remain hamstrung above the 8.5 percent level.
The median forecast of the 33 economists Reuters surveyed was for a fall in employment of 7,500 in September, and an unemployment rate of 8.6 percent.
Forecasts for the employment change ranged from a fall of 30,000 to a rise of 20,000, while the unemployment rate was forecast at between 8.5 and 8.8 percent.

With the ANZ job advertisment series, released on Monday, pointing to soft employment growth in the next six months, the continuing weakness in the labour market should support expectations of a rate cut in November.
"Continued modest employment growth and trend deterioration in unemployment would clearly support expectations for a rate cut," AMP Investments chief economist Shane Oliver said.

The expected fall would come after a 37,900 rise in August employment, boosted by the inclusion of 10,000 temporary workers for the national census. Their removal is a key factor behind the expected fall, economists said.

"We are expecting a correction to August's "outlier" employment growth partly from the finishing up of 10,000 Census workers and because the remaining 28,000 jobs created is inconsistent with the vacancy surveys," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
The markets will receive an update on inflation and wages in late October, and the general feeling amongst economists is that if these series show continued moderation, a November rate cut is likely.
Westpac senior economist John Peters was expecting a fall of around 10,000 to 15,000 in employment, and said such a result would enhance the bullish market tone.

"Such a result would further confirm still weak employment growth and point to the need for another easing in local policy settings soon, especially if wages and inflation pressures continue to trend lower," he said.
On Tuesday morning, December bill futures were trading at an implied yield about 48 points under the official cash rate, reflecting the market's expectation of a near term rate cut.
The outlook over the fourth quarter is for continued subdued jobs growth.
Economists surveyed by Reuters forecast monthly jobs growth in the December quarter to be around 11,000 a month.
The most optimistic saw monthly growth of 20,000, the least optimistic expected only 5,000 new jobs each month

The slow pace of employment growth -- seen by economists at just enough to match new entrants to the labour force -- would leave unemployment at 8.5 percent by year end, with some seeing it as high as 9.0 percent.
